sections.title: Cloud versus on-premises benefits
points: Cloud computing delivers compute, storage, networking and more over the internet, on demand, with pay-as-you-use pricing.
CapEx (up-front hardware and datacenter spend) shifts to OpEx (ongoing, pay-for-what-you-use spend).
Resources are provisioned rapidly and capacity scales up or down with demand; adding cloud capacity costs less than expanding a datacenter.
The provider uses virtualization to serve many customers from shared hardware; you do not need to own physical servers.
Drawbacks to know: cloud offers fewer custom configuration options than on-premises, and it does not reduce administrative complexity by itself.

sections.title: Public cloud and hybrid cloud advantage
points: Public cloud: owned and operated by a provider; hardware is shared by multiple organizations (tenants), each isolated from the others.
Public cloud is not owned by the public, is not open to every member of the public, and is not crowd-sourced.
Hybrid cloud: on-premises resources plus public cloud capacity; extends existing resources without buying a whole new datacenter.

sections.title: Cloud Adoption Framework stages
points: The Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure guides adoption in stages: Strategy, Plan, Ready, Adopt, then Govern and Manage.
Define strategy (business justification and outcomes) comes first; planning, readying the environment, and adopting follow.

sections.title: Who is always responsible for what
points: Provider always: physical datacenter, hosts and network.
Customer always: information and data, devices/endpoints, and accounts and identities.
Identity and directory infrastructure is shared in IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Customer responsibility is highest in IaaS, lower in PaaS, and lowest in SaaS.

sections.title: Responsibilities by service model
points: IaaS: customer manages OS, patching, applications and network controls; provider manages hardware and datacenter.
PaaS: provider manages OS and runtime; customer manages their application code and configuration, and user access; network controls are shared.
SaaS: provider runs the app, OS and infrastructure; customer configures the service, supplies data and manages access/identity.
Managed services such as Azure Backup are provider-operated platform services; you configure and use them.

sections.title: What moving to Azure VMs removes
points: Moving servers to Azure VMs (IaaS) eliminates hardware replacement and physical server security: the provider owns them.
Still yours on a VM: OS updates, application data backup and permissions to shared documents.

sections.title: Public cloud characteristics
points: Public cloud: all hardware is owned by the provider and shared between multiple tenants.
Characteristics: metered (pay-per-use) pricing, self-service management, no CapEx for hardware; not dedicated hardware.
An organization fully on the public cloud no longer needs its own datacenter; a private cloud or hybrid cloud still does.
Public cloud resources are virtual; you cannot add your own physical servers to it.

sections.title: Private cloud characteristics
points: Private cloud: resources used by one organization, often in its own datacenter; it gives complete control over resources and security.
A private cloud does not have to be disconnected from the internet.
Physical servers can be deployed in a private cloud or the on-premises part of a hybrid cloud, not in the public cloud.
Scaling a VM in the public cloud adds no capital expenditure for the customer; the provider carries it.

sections.title: Hybrid cloud
points: Hybrid cloud: combines on-premises (or private) resources with public cloud and lets workloads run in either place.
It requires an internal/on-premises network and a public cloud part; you can reach it by starting with public cloud, not only from a private cloud.
Typical examples: on-premises and Azure VMs connected together; an Azure web app querying an on-premises SQL Server.
It can extend internal capacity using public cloud resources.

sections.title: Choosing a cloud model by advantage
points: Public: no capital expenditure; pay for what you use.
Private: complete control over security and resources.
Hybrid: choice of on-premises or cloud-based resources.

sections.title: Matching workloads to cloud models
points: Public cloud: variable or growing demand, no hardware investment, fast provisioning.
Private cloud: need full control over hardware and security, or must keep resources on-premises.
Hybrid cloud: mix of both; keep some workloads on-premises and use the public cloud for extra capacity or specific services.

sections.title: Expenditure models
points: CapEx: up-front spending on physical infrastructure. OpEx: ongoing spending on services, paid as used.
Azure pay-as-you-go and other consumption-based cloud services are OpEx.
Elastic and scalable describe capabilities, not expenditure models.

sections.title: Consumption-based pricing
points: Consumption-based: you pay only for the resources you use, and can start or stop at any time; there is no fixed charge for unused capacity.
Pay-as-you-go is a consumption-based model; costs fall because you pay for extra capacity only when needed.
Serverless computing is an example of consumption-based pricing.

sections.title: CapEx versus OpEx examples
points: CapEx: building a datacenter, buying servers and other physical infrastructure.
OpEx: pay-as-you-go cloud usage, electricity, staff salaries, leasing or subscribing to software.
Migrating to Azure pay-as-you-go moves spending from CapEx to OpEx.

sections.title: Planning for Azure costs
points: Azure uses pay-as-you-go pricing.
A migrated website therefore brings recurring monthly usage costs, not an up-front purchase.

sections.title: Azure Functions
points: Azure Functions: serverless compute that runs your code in response to events (triggers) without you managing servers.
Functions are stateless by default; Durable Functions add state.
Not serverless: virtual machines, storage accounts and dedicated hosts.

sections.title: Azure Logic Apps
points: Logic Apps: serverless workflows built from triggers and actions using connectors, with little or no code.
Fits rule-based automation such as sending email notifications when an event occurs.
Compare: Functions runs code you write; Logic Apps orchestrates a workflow.

sections.title: High availability and fault tolerance
points: High availability: a service stays accessible with minimal downtime when a component fails; built into many platform services such as Azure SQL Data Warehouse.
Availability zones: separate datacenters in a region; spread VMs across zones to survive a datacenter failure.
Availability sets protect against rack and host failures, within one datacenter.

sections.title: Vertical versus horizontal scaling
points: Vertical scaling (scale up): add CPU or memory to an existing VM.
Horizontal scaling (scale out): add more instances, such as extra VMs; it can happen automatically or manually.
A service that supports more instances (20 versus 5) is more scalable.
Scaling to match demand also helps control costs.

sections.title: Elasticity and autoscaling
points: Elasticity: resources are allocated and released automatically as demand changes.
Autoscaling, such as VM scale sets, is elasticity.
Elasticity suits uneven usage (a heavy final week each month): you pay only for the capacity you use.

sections.title: Matching cloud benefits to needs
points: High availability: continuous user experience if a resource fails. Fault tolerance: stays available after a component fails.
Disaster recovery: restore a service after an outage (backup, replication).
Scalability/dynamic scalability: increase capacity as demand grows. Elasticity: do so dynamically.
Agility: quickly deploy, configure and adapt resources. Geo-distribution: deploy to regions close to users. Low latency: fast access.
Predictability covers performance and cost; manageability covers management of and in the cloud.

sections.title: Azure Machine Learning
points: Azure Machine Learning is the Azure service to build, train, test and deploy machine learning models.
It is the service to use for predictive analytics and AI solutions.

sections.title: Reliability and fault tolerance
points: Reliability: the system recovers from failures and keeps working.
Fault tolerance: a service stays available through a failure, including loss of a datacenter, by using redundant components across datacenters.
Elasticity, scalability and low latency address demand and speed, not failure.

sections.title: Predictability
points: Predictability covers performance: consistent behavior under load.
Predictability also covers cost: you can forecast and calculate what a service will cost.

sections.title: Azure Site Recovery
points: Azure Site Recovery provides disaster recovery for virtual machines by replicating them to a secondary region.
Disaster recovery restores a service after an outage; high availability keeps it running.

sections.title: Security and governance in the cloud
points: Cloud services can meet security, governance and compliance needs with built-in tools and templates.
Governance includes setting standards and auditing resources for compliance.
Security is shared: the provider secures the infrastructure; you secure your data and access.

sections.title: Manageability in the cloud
points: Management of the cloud: autoscaling, templates, monitoring and alerts to run resources.
Management in the cloud: portal, CLI, PowerShell and APIs to manage resources.

sections.title: Reducing administrative effort
points: Azure Reserved VM Instances are a pricing discount for a 1- or 3-year commitment; they do not reduce administration.
To cut the effort of deploying many VMs, use automation, templates or scale sets.

sections.title: IaaS characteristics
points: IaaS: you rent virtual infrastructure: VMs, storage and networks. Azure virtual machines are the standard example.
You install and manage the operating system, so IaaS fits lift-and-shift migrations.
PaaS and SaaS do not let you install an OS.

sections.title: When to choose IaaS
points: Choose IaaS for apps with prerequisite software, legacy databases or custom OS configuration.
You need full control of the server; the provider only manages hardware.

sections.title: PaaS characteristics
points: PaaS: a managed platform where you deploy code and the provider manages OS and infrastructure; no control of the host OS.
Azure App Service can scale automatically (autoscale), and memory/CPU is increased by changing the pricing tier.
You maintain application code; PaaS minimizes administrative effort for web apps.

sections.title: Identifying PaaS resources
points: PaaS examples: Azure App Service, Azure SQL Database, Azure Cosmos DB.
A SQL Server you install on a VM is IaaS; Azure SQL Database is managed by Azure.
A PaaS-only plan cannot include VMs; Storage accounts are not counted as PaaS here.

sections.title: SaaS characteristics
points: SaaS: provider-hosted, ready-to-use software; customer responsibility is smallest.
Microsoft 365 is SaaS; IaaS and PaaS require more management.

sections.title: Classifying Azure services
points: IaaS: Azure virtual machines, a DNS server on a VM, SQL Server on a VM.
PaaS: Azure App Service, Azure Functions, Azure SQL Database, Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Files.
SaaS: Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, Microsoft Intune.

sections.title: Picking the model for a requirement
points: IaaS: most control; hosts VMs; suits cloud file servers.
PaaS: custom apps with minimal OS effort; databases without OS maintenance.
SaaS: ready-made apps such as an accounting system.
Deploying virtual machines is IaaS, not PaaS or SaaS.
Need to change code but not manage the OS: PaaS. Need to work with the server OS: IaaS.
